title: Theravada Buddhism
summary: Theravada traces itself to the third century BCE, when the Mauryan emperor Ashoka called a Buddhist council at Pataliputra and supported missions abroad; his son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitta are credited with bringing Theravada and its canon to Sri Lanka. It holds the Pali canon as its highest scripture and Pali as its sacred language. In the twelfth century Sri Lanka's Mahavihara lineage became the model of orthodoxy, sought out by monks from mainland Southeast Asia. It is now the main Buddhism of Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia.

uncertainty.note: Traditional establishment dated to the Third Buddhist Council during the reign of Mauryan Emperor Ashoka (c. 268-232 BCE) and Mahinda's mission to Sri Lanka in the third century BCE.

where.modern_name: Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka (stand-in pin for the Sri Lankan centre of early Theravada)

importance.justification: The Buddhism of Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia for two millennia (R3 D3 T4 L2).

related.because: Ashoka called the third Buddhist council at Pataliputra and supported missionaries, including his son Mahinda, who brought Buddhism to Sri Lanka (UW Silk Road; Encyclopedia of Religion).

beats.caption: In the third century BCE, Emperor Ashoka supported the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra and dispatched monastic missions.
Mahinda introduced the Theravada lineage and Pali canon to Sri Lanka, establishing the foundation for its spread to Southeast Asia.
